Maybe talk about recording. You’ve done so much recording. What, for you, makes the recording session a success?

It’s something that happens to everybody in the studio. At one point it happens that everybody, they become committed. Once that commitment is made, then the music sounds completely different all the way. That’s what occurs and you have to be able to bring that out. I think it takes time and that’s all. Sometimes an hour, sometimes ten- minutes, but when that happens you don’t have any problems.
It seems like it’s easier to do that on the bandstand than it is in the recording studio. Is that?

Well on the bandstand you’ve got an audience to play for. In the studio you’re simply making a record and it’s impersonal. That’s the difference. There is nobody there but yourself actually. That’s what makes the difference. Once you make that commitment, then the music is together. Then the rapport is possible. Everything else…you’re ready to play the music.
So what do you look for, what are the criteria; what are the qualities in a musician you look for, to bring them into the Elvin Jones Ensemble? What are the things you’re looking for in a musician?

Well, first they have to be, they have to be, a certain amount of maturity has to be there within whoever the guy is. They understand what the command of the instrument is all about. A lot of people want jobs but they’re not prepared. You know, they haven’t studied enough, they haven’t….they don’t know the scales. And if you don’t know the scales then you’re not ready to play with anybody. That’s important that they know, that they know about to do and they’ve prepared themselves for that. Same if you’ve made an audition for the Philharmonic. What’s the difference?

There is the issue of technical facility but what about a particular artistic vision? Particularly in jazz, you have to be able to improvise so you have to make a statement as well as being able to play somebody else’s music. So, how do you play…how do you judge somebody’s solo or improvisational ability?

Well if you hear ‘em play that should tell you. That gives you all the information you need if they can come in and be a part of that orchestra. Not even for any reward or anything like that. “Oh you’re going to have the job for four or six months” or “Oh we’re

going into the studio and record.” It’s not that. You have to know how to play. You have to know, to be… As I said, that’s part of being mature and being grown. You have to be adult with respects, so that you’re not what the people used to call a “shuck-in”. (Laughs) So you’re not shucking. When a cat is straight, he doesn’t have any problems. Usually people are very sincere about that.

I bring this up, and I’m glad that you qualify it, because there are many, many brilliant musicians but, as far as their sense of responsibility, or, like you say, the maturity, sure they’re technical wizards, they’re musical geniuses, but personally, they may be not able to make that type of commitment you talk about…
Exactly.
…that’s necessary to bring the group together. That must be something that you’re observing before they get in the group. I’m sure you’re observing, checking, and monitoring that.

I try to be sure that person is qualified before. I say, “This is not a jam session. We’re serious.” You have to be prepared for that. Normally I don’t have any problems because anytime someone comes to me they are more than ready. I’ve been lucky that way.

More often than not, the musicians will come to you and you’re able to select, rather than getting referrals from other musicians. What happens when one of your musicians can’t make the gig and they send in a sub? Do you have a process where you take the person at his word, or do you then meet that musician before you bring them in?

Well I think they should make sure that I know who the sub is before they do that. Because if somebody comes and say, “Okay I’m coming because Ed George sent me over.” Well I say, “You know this ain’t George’s band. You gotta, you know, we’ll play without you.” If I had to play a duet—it’s as simple as that. You can’t sacrifice yourself for no reason, and that’s a stupid reason. Just because somebody says, you know they’re dodging their responsibility and putting it on someone else.

So throughout your career you worked with some of the most accomplished musicians in this music. Obviously, you’re working with them as a sideman; you’re observing them as a bandleaders. Throughout your career as a bandleader, how were they influential, which ones were influential, and what did they give you, or what did you observe as far as being a bandleader? What are the traits that make a great bandleader, what are the things that you got through other people, or maybe observed from other people?

It’s a great many things, I think it’s more of … you have to have a natural understanding of the basic psychology of people. You know, you don’t scare somebody to death. They might be ready to play but they’re shy. So, it’s just that you have to be able to recognize what it is that that person is saying or representing, and see how truthful he is. You can usually tell if a person is truthful, and that’s enough.

Even though from 1967 on you became a bandleader, yet, you still continued to work on other people’s projects as a collaborator. This is seemingly a very rare and very remarkable gift to be able to be a bandleader and then to adapt and be a in a roll as a sideman or accompanist.
Yeah, absolutely.
Does this still suit you to this day?
You know, I’ll tell you it’s like they say in the Army, “A good leader wouldn’t tell his men to do something that he couldn’t do himself.” So it’s as simple as that.
Do you think you’ve retained any qualities or any training from the Army? Has any of that served you in this life as a musician?

Well it gave me a certain understanding of self-discipline. We all have to have that if we intend to grow up and mature as a man or as a person. You know, here you got a horn you say, “Do you know how to play it? I see you got a horn but do you know how to play it?” (Laughs) Somebody has to be…like some people can give it out but they can’t take it. It’s sort of like that

One thing that’s unique about you and the Elvin Jones Jazz Machine, unlike, say, Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers, he brings in young musicians and they play with him and then they go out. You have musicians that play with you, like Joe LaBarbera, who played with you, they come back, then they’re going to get some more Elvin then they go back out, and then they come back , and then they go out and then they come back. That’s very rare, that’s why I want to ask you these questions. As a bandleader you have a remarkable ability to bring these musicians back. You keep expanding what you’re doing, but you bring these musicians back even after they’ve gone out.

It’s the same thing that happens with Duke Ellington’s bands. I’ve seen Ben Webster walk out and six months later he comes back in and stands up and plays his solo. (Laughs) Duke thought that was perfectly alright, it’s better than not coming. That’s what it’s all about; you have to be generous in that sense. It’s trust. I trust the guys that work with me and they know it.

So the Elvin Jones Jazz Machine has been stem rolling for several decades. Ken Kimery and I first saw that group in 1980 in Mannheim, Germany. At that time you had Andrew White, Ari Brown, Ryo? Was he playing guitar?

Andy McCloud
Andy McCloud
Yeah Andy.

I didn’t have any particular vision for that group because we started, the Jazz Machine with Jimmy Garrison and Joe Farrell (Laughs).
(Laughs) Okay, it just didn’t have that name then?
Right!
But the idea and the concept was in place.

Yeah you just add or subtract from that. But it’s sort of if it’s meant to be, it will be. That means, that’s how much effort you’re going to put into it. If you’re wholehearted, if you’re ready to die for it, that’s what you’re meant to do. You certainly have to have that kind of courage.
Who have been some of the members of the Jazz Machine that you particularly have a fond memory of and anything, if you’d like to share that with us?
Well, all of them. (Laughs)
(Laughs) Okay!

I don’t know anybody that I can pick one over the other. There’s been a lot of people, we’ve enjoyed each other’s company for many years on different occasions. We experienced things together. I try and tell guys, “When we are on the road you have to look out for your colleague. You keep your eye on him; he’ll keep his eye on you.” That means you learn how to love each other, and take care of each other, and be responsible in certain ways. That’s always part of the lesson. (Laughs)

Maybe I asked the wrong question in asking which people were memorable, I could ask about certain recordings. I have here an album that I wasn’t aware of, but I saw as an import, “Very Rare”. That’s almost praying to God for forgiveness.
How did you write this piece? Was it based on a Japanese folk song?

What’s your musical training?
I grew up with violin. My father loved the classical music and the folk song except we have no local teacher; we don’t know anything about it.
Are you talking about Western or Japanese folk song, or Western classical music?

We only know Japanese; we don’t know anything about the Western world. Nothing. So that’s it. Then jazz come around early ‘50’s so you know. I listen to it, I grew up with it. I mentioned before I like haiku and story and poet and I like to sing also. Every time I sing it’s never recorded. I’m just lucky. We have a project, some very famous projects that say they want to record only my tunes because every time seems like a hit. You know, Django Brothers, and all this, and other musicians asking me to make arrangements. But it’s only idea that comes from Elvin’s drums; it doesn’t come from saxophone or piano. Only the drum, so instead of piano I got a snare drum.

Again, when we went to see you in Mannheim, Germany in 1980 I remember very distinctly, first Keiko comes out, sets up the drums, tunes the drums. Keiko tell us how you got to be not only the drum-tech, but the drum tuner?

Well she knows how to say get out better than anyone! (Laughs)
I am concentrated, very serious. When drummer comes up and asks me I say, “You have to find your own ear of sound.”

They closed the bridge.

They closed the bridge and I said, “I smell something funny.” He say, “Yeah.” Elvin was very quiet. I say, “Driver let’s go home,” he say, “Yeah but the doctor.” I say, “Don’t worry about doctor.” We made a drum clinic for the doctor, for days later.
Yeah it was Barry’s, over at Barry’s.
Four days later?
Well people started coming out. I said, “Well, what are they afraid of?” They gotta keep living.

The great hell has passed and they have something to listen to: Elvin playing the drums. I can’t even talk at that. It was terrible. I said, “Elvin what is this? Joke or movie?” Friend of mine was taking video. He cannot believe that these are people falling. He look up and smoke. I hear that he made lots of money because he sold tape.
What did you think when you saw that Elvin? What went through your mind?

I first thought, cause I recall when…in the 40’s when that B-25 bomber hit the Empire State Building on the 70th floor and killed a lot of people, but it didn’t do the damage that these did. And I thought, I said, “Well you know, the sky is clear. It couldn’t be, they couldn’t have done it by mistake. Somebody trying to land a LaGuardia airport and they got of course or something.” Then I said, “Well, no, that’s deliberate. Somebody just did that.” Then you find out that all these planes got hijacked so that solved that riddle. That’s terrible and before that, before they had that bomb, this truck bomb, we were there a day before. I saw all of these policemen and I say “What is this?” They didn’t say anything; there‘s like 100 cops out there. The next day, “Bang!” They should have…if they had stayed there it wouldn’t have happened (Laughs). You really can’t prevent things sometimes. Most times you can’t. If anyone is determined, they’re going to do it anyway. They do or die, that’s their philosophy. You know, to me, I always think about what is their philosophy about religion? And everybody claims to be this, and it’s got the tenderness of loving each other, and this is practically all religions. So what do they do in Israel? They leave the mosque and they go blow up a house? I don’t see any religion there? That isn’t God’s work, that’s the devil. That’s not God.
Do have any views or any concept of what’s going on in this world? Keiko is saying, “There is another one coming.”
Oh it’s coming. I just hope it’s not the nuclear bomb.
Are we finished? Cause…
Oh I was just going to ask you about the Blue Note date. When I was here last month, you gave a drum master class at the Manhattan School of Music.
Right.
I wasn’t able to attend cause I had to go to this other one over at Columbia. But how did that go? I heard a lot of great things.

It went great. Like a lot of the student body, they brought instruments in. Trumpet players, and saxophone players, and two trombonists, and there was a bass player from Puerto Rico. They wanted to jam; they wanted to have a session. Part of my lecture was

that I enjoy playing with anybody. (Laughs) So we had a great time on stage, they just came up and had some fun. They loved it! Especially when you get a kid that’s reluctant sort of, he’s a little shy or something, it’s hard to come out of their shell. But if you can do it, you can hear something that comes from inside of them. And that’s what I heard, all these kids, everybody took a solo. It was great.

What happens when… I don’t know if there any students you’ve had for a long period of time that you can say yes that, or they can say yes that they’ve studied with Elvin Jones maybe more than one or two lessons. What do you do with a student when you’re trying to nurture them and bring them along?

I try to get them to… they have to admit what they want. It isn’t what I can give them, it’s what they want. What can I do to help them understand the problem they’re trying to solve. That’s the role of a teacher. When they begin to understand that it just, all of the problems dissolve.
Just like you mentioned Charlie Persip was studying with Sam Woodyard, is there anybody that can say, “Oh I studied with Elvin Jones.” Is there anybody? Can we keep our eyes out for them?

There’s a lot of guys. I used to teach down at Frank Ippolito, upstairs there. Frank was teaching there and Norman Grossman from Manus College. The three of us, we had these kids, these students coming in. So I ran into one of my students who lives in California, out in Los Angeles. Every time we play at the Jazz Bakery he comes in. He brought all of his kids, his son! Big boys! They’re grown up now. He’s got dozens of students and he always comes by to say hello. He always comes to see me. Ken Kimery: Did you teach Adam Nussbaum anytime?
He took a lesson but I didn’t teach him. Adam Nussbaum was curious but I didn’t think he was serious.
What’s that students name out in Los Angeles?
Lennie something. What’s his last name?
Very serious, we have become so proud of him.
What years were you teaching?
1972? Just one year?
Yes. About eight months. We were broke; we had to make money at some point. He was teaching up to five students

And now to really bring this to a close, next week Elvin Jones at the Blue Note. And, as Keiko said, in December. So what are we in store for if I can make it back? Elvin Jones, I know you’re doing the two second sets with Cecil Taylor?
Then you’ll see me playing from a wheel chair. (Laughs)
No! (Laughs) That’s terrible!
After Cecil gets through with me! Enjoy it!
Yeah, sure! On a throne, whether it’s the drummer’s throne or a rolling throne, you’re on it. (Laughs) Okay well I think the table is being set!
Well while I think she’s getting everything set here I can take you downstairs.
Oh great! END OF INTERVIEW Transcribed by Kyle Kelly-Yahner

segments.title: Opening of the interview at Elvin and Keiko Jones's apartment
segments.summary: Anthony Brown announces the date, place and people present and asks Elvin to state his name and birth.

segments.title: Born in Pontiac as a twin; parents from Vicksburg
segments.summary: Elvin was born in 1927, his twin Elvin Roy died at six months, and his parents Henry and Olivia came from Vicksburg, Mississippi.

segments.title: His brothers and sisters; Olivvia drowns
segments.summary: Elvin lists his sisters and brothers, tells of Olivvia drowning through the ice, and says only he and Hank survive.

segments.title: Music at home and the Baptist church
segments.summary: His mother taught herself piano and spirituals; the family went to church, and his father was a deacon at Trinity Baptist.

segments.title: His father's work as a lumber inspector for General Motors
segments.summary: Elvin explains his father picked the lumber used in car and bus frames, and when the family left Vicksburg.

segments.title: The houses and neighborhood in Pontiac
segments.summary: He names the three houses he lived in and describes the business-district neighborhood near the church.

segments.title: Working in his uncle's dry-cleaning shop; carpentry from his father
segments.summary: He worked for his uncle Joseph, fell into the carbon tetrachloride tank, and learned carpentry watching his father.

segments.title: Grade school, friends and sports
segments.summary: He disliked starting school, had a friend who taught him to swim, ran track and played softball and football.

segments.title: A working-class, integrated neighborhood
segments.summary: He describes a mixed neighborhood of many languages where neighbors helped each other and the schools were integrated.

segments.title: His mother's work and the family singing
segments.summary: His mother cleaned offices for $2 a week and bought Hank a piano; the children sang spirituals and quartets at home, and Olivvia taught voice.

segments.title: The WPA band: Hank, Uncle Bill and the tuba player
segments.summary: Listening to Hank's WPA band rehearse at their house made Elvin want to play, with its tuba player on a bicycle and drummer Juve Baby.

segments.title: Circuses and parades draw him to the drums
segments.summary: The circus grounds in front of the house and the drum sections of parades captivated him and he wanted no other instrument.

segments.title: Mr. Weist and the Paul Yoder drum method
segments.summary: In junior high band director Fred Weist started him on percussion; he read the Yoder book overnight and was moved to the first band.

segments.title: Practicing and school band repertoire
segments.summary: He had no drum of his own, practiced on a pad until he mastered the roll, played marches, and was kept home at night by his mother.

segments.title: Hearing Ellington records at a neighbor's house
segments.summary: A neighbor's Duke Ellington and Johnny Hodges records hooked him, and he recalls the WPA band drummers.

segments.title: School percussion and no drum set
segments.summary: He played bass drum, cymbals and bell lyre at school and mostly marches, with no set until after the Air Force.

segments.title: Pontiac's size and joining the Boy Scouts
segments.summary: He gives the town's population and describes a World War I veteran scoutmaster who taught discipline.

segments.title: Serving as drum major; Weist's influence
segments.summary: He learned baton and marching signals as drum major, and Mr. Weist's strict advice to practice until the muscles stop aching shaped him.

segments.title: Leaving school and home for Boston and New York
segments.summary: He left school in 10th grade, worked in a factory, then left home for Boston and New York, taking laundry jobs before joining the Army.

segments.title: The paper route with Arthur Hoseppian
segments.summary: Elvin recalls taking over a friend's paper route in junior high, giving papers free to families on welfare, and how friends fared in the war.

segments.title: Enlisting in 1946; Fort Dix and Fort Lee band school
segments.summary: He enlisted wanting an Army or Air Corps band, trained at Fort Dix, then the military band school at Fort Lee where he taught.

segments.title: Transfer to the 766th Army Air Corps band
segments.summary: He was transferred to the Air Corps band in Columbus, Ohio, after teaching drum cadences at Fort Lee, and says he loved Army life.

segments.title: Segregated units and bandleader Mr. Bryce
segments.summary: He recalls integrated band school but a segregated Columbus unit, with a bandleader who reminded him of Weist.

segments.title: Marimba with Ragland and playing bass drum
segments.summary: Besides duty he studied marimba with a Columbus Symphony percussionist and chose the bass drum for its role in the cadence.

segments.title: Special Services show and working as a stagehand
segments.summary: He explains the Special Services unit that formed a touring stage show, where he was stagehand rather than a band member.

segments.title: Hearing Sid Catlett and bebop on records
segments.summary: A record of Dizzy Gillespie's 'Salt Peanuts' with Sid Catlett's brushes convinced him he had to play drum set, and he names the new drummers.

segments.title: Operation Happiness and subbing for Perry Reed
segments.summary: He organized the show Operation Happiness, learned big-band playing from drummer Perry Reed, and took his place; he was discharged as T/5.

segments.title: His father's death and furlough home
segments.summary: Called home by the Red Cross, Elvin bathes his dying father, who had cancer at 63, and the family gathers.

segments.title: Buying his first drum set and practicing with Hank
segments.summary: He returned to his mother's house, paid cash for a Ludwig set bought in Detroit, and Hank taught him to play along with Art Tatum records.

segments.title: Drummers he tried to learn from
segments.summary: He heard Kenny Clarke, Sonny Greer, Buddy Rich and Krupa, and says the point was to find what he could do rather than copy.

segments.title: Art Martigan and the Crystal Lounge: first job with Wardell Gray
segments.summary: Going to Detroit he met drummer Art Martigan, who handed him the six-night Crystal Lounge job with Wardell Gray.

segments.title: Odd jobs and washing used cars
segments.summary: Before music paid he pressed clothes and ran a car wash rack beside used car lots.

segments.title: Crystal Lounge routine; Phil Hill's band and the lost pay
segments.summary: The Crystal Lounge was a jazz club with long sets; when Phil Hill took over the band he ran off with the week's pay in the snow.

segments.title: Backing Charlie Parker for two weeks
segments.summary: Owner Edward Bertrand had Elvin form a trio with Barry Harris to back Charlie Parker, who played effortlessly and died soon after.

segments.title: Moving to the Bluebird Inn with Billy Mitchell
segments.summary: He clarifies the timeline from his discharge and describes the neighborhood Bluebird Inn on Tireman where he worked over three years.

segments.title: First recording with Thad Jones and Billy Mitchell
segments.summary: He describes recording for David Usher's label in a noisy second-floor studio, uneasy with microphones, and the uncertain date.

segments.title: Miles Davis in Detroit; stays at the Joneses' house
segments.summary: Miles came to the Bluebird without a band, and Elvin played with him for six months while he stayed at Elvin's house.

segments.title: Monday jam picnics at home and the cat Black Night
segments.summary: Elvin describes weekly jazz picnics at his Detroit house and his cat who slept by the bass drum.

segments.title: Checking the dates of Crystal Lounge, Parker and Miles
segments.summary: Brown and Elvin work out the order of events, with Parker in winter and Miles the following summer.

segments.title: Miles Davis as a player and composer
segments.summary: What impressed Elvin most was how well Miles played and his unique concept of composition.

segments.title: Miles getting himself together and losing his voice
segments.summary: Elvin says Miles came to Detroit to recover from drugs, had a throat operation, ignored advice not to drink and lost his voice.

segments.title: The Benny Goodman audition in New York
segments.summary: Hank recommended Elvin for Benny Goodman's world tour and he flew to New York to read Gene Krupa's 'Sing, Sing, Sing' part.

segments.title: The Rouge Lounge with Kenny Burrell, Barry Harris and Carmen McRae
segments.summary: He describes the River Rouge bowling-alley club and the group he worked with before leaving for New York.

segments.title: Kenny Clarke and his practice-pad book
segments.summary: Staying in Hank's hotel room, Elvin met Kenny Clarke, whom he calls the granddaddy of the music, and discusses his classic style.

segments.title: Philly Joe Jones
segments.summary: He recalls meeting Philly Joe, his Boris Karloff imitation, finger technique and dynamics.

segments.title: Calls from Mingus, Miles and Sauter-Finegan
segments.summary: He met other New York drummers, then received calls the next day, and Mingus had him learn his book and form a quartet.

segments.title: Touring with Mingus and Teddy Charles; first Newport Festival
segments.summary: The quartet played Music Inn, Washington and Newport with Mingus and Teddy Charles constantly arguing.

segments.title: Staying in the union and not playing for nothing
segments.summary: He did not hang out for free sessions in New York and transferred his Detroit union card without trouble.

segments.title: Cecil Taylor and Steve Lacy's recollection
segments.summary: Elvin confirms he sought out Cecil Taylor when others left the stand and calls Cecil far ahead of everyone.

segments.title: Roy Haynes and Birdland Mondays
segments.summary: He recalls meeting Roy Haynes at the Michigan State Fair and later seeing him in New York.

segments.title: Teddy Charles in Toronto and Bud Powell
segments.summary: After Toronto Mingus took him to Cleveland to play with Bud Powell, then Detroit and Birdland over a few months.

segments.title: A piano-less trio with Lee Konitz
segments.summary: He recorded with Lee Konitz and Sonny Dallas and says playing without piano is no challenge.

segments.title: 'Mad Thad' session of January 1957
segments.summary: Asked about the Thad Jones date, he says he was no longer afraid of microphones and describes his approach to accompaniment.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Playing with Tyree Glenn at the Roundtable
segments.summary: Before J.J. he worked about a year with Tyree Glenn's trombone-and-vibes group at the Roundtable.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Records for J.J. Johnson and the boat to Europe
segments.summary: J.J. recorded 'J is for Jazz' at Columbia before the tour, and Elvin enjoyed sailing on the S.S. Stockholm.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Scandinavian tour with J.J.: 50,000 in Stockholm
segments.summary: The tour began in Copenhagen, drew 50,000 to the Kungstradgarden in Stockholm, and lasted three months from Lapland to Gothenburg.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Sonny Rollins at the Village Vanguard
segments.summary: Back from tour and out with his brother Tom, Elvin was pulled on stage by Rollins and learned it was a Blue Note recording.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Fired by J.J. and carrying a pistol
segments.summary: He explains he left J.J.'s band after an argument in Philadelphia, and says he carried a pistol since age 17.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: The argument with J.J. Johnson
segments.summary: J.J. accused him of not keeping time, and Elvin suspects another motive.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Work and recordings after the Vanguard, 1957-58
segments.summary: Brown reviews recordings and Elvin recalls gigs with Pepper Adams and Donald Byrd.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Opening of the second day of interview
segments.summary: Brown announces the date June 11 and the start of part two.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: The exotic dancer job with Jo Jo McKinney
segments.summary: After the Phil Hill episode Elvin briefly played for a dancer and a singer with no pitch.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Playing drum set in the Air Force; Perry Reed again
segments.summary: He confirms he never played other service bands, that his stagehand job let him learn the show, and he subbed on the drum set.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Going home for his father's illness
segments.summary: He explains the Red Cross furlough, his short stay in Pontiac and the bus trips back to base.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: His mother's heart disease and death
segments.summary: His mother, with heart disease, died on the stairs on Thanksgiving three years after his father.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Recording with Thad and Hank, and playing with his brothers
segments.summary: Elvin says the Jones brothers' record was their first together and that he worked with Thad only as an adult at the Bluebird.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Tyree Glenn's Roundtable quartet and the hundred-dollar bills
segments.summary: He took Poppa Joe Jones's place in Tyree's group, played requests like 'Saints', and a customer laid $680 on his tom-tom.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Tyree Glenn and his band
segments.summary: Elvin describes Tyree's vibes playing, personality, CBS staff job, and the group with Flanagan and Potter.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Monk's Montreal trip with a substitute drummer
segments.summary: Sonny Rollins told him Monk wanted him in Montreal that day, so Elvin got Kenny Dennis to sub and went with Monk, with the bass player missing.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Knowing Monk and hearing Coltrane at the Five Spot
segments.summary: He had listened at the Five Spot to Monk with Wilbur Ware and Shadow Wilson, and first heard Coltrane there.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Dating the Monk trip; leaving Tyree for J.J.
segments.summary: Elvin works out the chronology and says he left Tyree for J.J.'s recordings and Scandinavian tour, getting the years muddled.

segments.chapter: Sideman years: J.J., Tyree Glenn, Sweets
segments.title: Touring with Harry 'Sweets' Edison
segments.summary: Sweets used him as a sub, and the quartet toured the eastern and midwestern circuit for a year or more until 1959.

segments.title: Choosing Coltrane over Dizzy Gillespie
segments.summary: Elvin had accepted Dizzy's offer when Coltrane called, got a release from Dizzy, and chose Trane because he wanted to play with him.

segments.title: First night with Coltrane in Denver, replacing Billy Higgins
segments.summary: He joined the Coltrane quartet in Denver after Billy Higgins played the first set, hearing 'My Favorite Things'.

segments.title: The Denver club and the quartet's silence
segments.summary: He recalls the nearly empty Denver club and compares the quartet to the Budapest String Quartet, who did not speak.

segments.title: 'My Favorite Things' and 'Blues to Elvin'
segments.summary: Back in New York they recorded 'My Favorite Things'; the 'Blues to Elvin' tune led to talk of his guitar.

segments.title: Learning guitar from Red the bootlegger
segments.summary: Elvin tells how he picked up a little guitar from a man who ran a bootleg bar near his uncle's cleaners.

segments.title: Coltrane's early bass players: Steve Davis, Reggie Workman, Art Davis
segments.summary: He describes the revolving bass chairs, including the two-bass pairing he compared to a hornets' nest.

segments.title: Bringing Jimmy Garrison into the band
segments.summary: He says Jimmy Garrison came shortly after, the group came together, and he pushed Trane to choose Garrison.

segments.title: His first Riverside date as a leader
segments.summary: He explains the album 'Elvin', the missing cover photo that led him to Roy DeCarava, and the help from Thad, Hank and others.

segments.title: Not wanting to be a bandleader
segments.summary: He stayed with Coltrane because he was learning, and could not think of horn players for a group of his own.

segments.title: Eric Dolphy
segments.summary: He remembers Dolphy from Mingus's band, his command of the horn, and his honey eating.

segments.title: First European tour with Coltrane: the shopping-bag luggage
segments.summary: He recalls going to Europe with Trane with dirty shirts and a shopping bag instead of a suitcase.

segments.title: European audiences and treatment compared with the US
segments.summary: He says no crowd matched J.J.'s 50,000, praises subsidized European clubs, and contrasts the hospitality with the US.

segments.title: Always bringing his own drums
segments.summary: He travels with his own drums after breaking bass drum heads and sticks on borrowed sets.

segments.title: Treatment in Louisville and missing Coltrane dates
segments.summary: He explains absences covered by Roy Haynes and Jack DeJohnette as time in a federal facility for addicts in Louisville.

segments.title: Knowing the quartet's music was extraordinary
segments.summary: He says he always knew Coltrane was special from hearing him with Monk, and the quartet continued that development.

segments.title: How Coltrane introduced new tunes without charts
segments.summary: Trane played tunes for the band, no charts, and the rhythm section listened until it could play; Elvin changed rhythms freely.

segments.title: 'Chasin' the Trane' and the Gothenburg concert
segments.summary: He says Trane first played the long duet with drums in Gothenburg, and Elvin did not dare stop.

segments.title: Coltrane's way of directing the band
segments.summary: After a break, he says Trane spoke through the bell of the horn, and the 'Sun Ship' remark was rare.

segments.title: Coltrane's study of India, Ravi Shankar and tabla
segments.summary: Trane's interest in Indian music and Africa came indirectly; Elvin discusses tabla, which he never learned.

segments.title: Olatunji, and Elvin's own trip to Guinea and Senegal
segments.summary: He remembers Babatunde Olatunji at the Village Gate and describes a gathering of master drummers in Guinea.

segments.title: Elvin's own listening: Bobby Timmons, pygmy recordings, classical
segments.summary: He tells of Bobby Timmons's pygmy record and says he loves Stravinsky and Casals.

segments.title: Coltrane's 'Alabama'
segments.summary: He recalls Trane writing and playing 'Alabama' after the church bombing.

segments.title: 'A Love Supreme' in the studio
segments.summary: He says Trane arrived at the studio and simply started playing, and 'A Love Supreme' was playful.

segments.title: The 'Crescent' drum solo and soloing approach
segments.summary: Elvin describes being told to play a solo and says he must feel in control, embellishing the tune.

segments.title: Drums and cymbals as color
segments.summary: He explains the cymbals' tones, closing his eyes to see rainbows, and tuning drums like crayons.

segments.title: The documentary 'A Different Drummer'
segments.summary: Elvin recalls a student filmmaker making the documentary over five years, finishing in 1979.

segments.title: The 'Three Card Molly' idea in 1957
segments.summary: Asked about a signature figure heard in 1957, he says developed ideas can be reached for later.

segments.title: Developing his signature style
segments.summary: He says he never consciously aimed for a signature and that ideas take years; perfect moments are rare.

segments.title: Playback and the leader's decisions
segments.summary: He listens to playbacks mainly to balance sound, and only the leader decides on retakes.

segments.title: The spiritual turn after 'A Love Supreme' and Elvin's focus
segments.summary: He links the music's spirituality to Coltrane's children and says his own life focus was playing without mistakes.

segments.title: Coltrane's expanding group in 1965
segments.summary: Elvin describes Trane's religious reading, shakuhachi, and the arrival of Pharaoh Sanders, Archie Shepp and Rashied Ali.

segments.title: The conflict with Rashied Ali over drums
segments.summary: He left Trane in 1966 after friction when Rashied moved his drums at the Village Gate.

segments.title: Quitting in San Francisco and the call from Duke Ellington's nephew
segments.summary: He left Trane's stage with a headache, and Steve James then called him to join Duke Ellington in Spain.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
segments.title: Tape four: why Poppa Joe Jones recommended him to Tyree Glenn
segments.summary: Asked about Joe Jones, Elvin says Joe knew him from Frank Ippolito's drum shop.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
segments.title: Gil Evans and 'Sketches of Spain'
segments.summary: He recalls rehearsing with Gil Evans and learning castanets from a flamenco dancer for 'Sketches of Spain'.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
segments.title: Gil Evans and Miles Davis
segments.summary: He says Miles insisted on Gil Evans as arranger and Gil was serene and a genius.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
segments.title: Joining Duke Ellington's tour in Frankfurt
segments.summary: He agreed to join Duke in Frankfurt, was one of two drummers, and disliked the heavy back beat of the other.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
segments.title: Playing with Ellington's band; Sam Woodyard
segments.summary: He was asked to play in Milan, was paid six weeks for three, and the band's visitors came to see him in Boston.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
segments.title: The Ellington and Coltrane session
segments.summary: He recalls first meeting Duke at the Ellington-Coltrane date, where Duke improvised a ditty.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
segments.title: Sam Woodyard
segments.summary: He explains he already knew Sam Woodyard through Charlie Persip and admired his energy and passion.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
segments.title: Art Blakey
segments.summary: He praises Blakey's playing with Monk, his press roll, and recalls sitting in for him at Sweet Basil.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
segments.title: Remembering the Montreal gig with Monk and Charlie Rouse
segments.summary: Elvin was thrilled to play with Monk and Charlie Rouse and recalls 'Misterioso'.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
segments.title: Forming a trio with Jimmy Garrison and Joe Farrell
segments.summary: After the Ellington tour he formed a piano-less trio, which recorded 'Putting It Together'.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
segments.title: McCoy Tyner leaving Coltrane; Elvin's departure from San Francisco
segments.summary: He says he did not discuss his plans, thought Alice's wish to play may have prompted McCoy, then flew to Europe.

segments.chapter: Ellington, Gil Evans and first own groups
segments.title: Why piano-less; Pookie's Pub and the Vanguard
segments.summary: He explains no pianist was available, and describes working at Pookie's Pub with Coltrane visiting.

segments.title: Meeting Keiko in 1962
segments.summary: Elvin recounts seeing Keiko in a kimono with flowers at Birdland, then not meeting again for four years.

segments.title: Meeting again in Nagasaki on the drum-battle tour
segments.summary: They met again on George Wein's Japan tour with Blakey, Tony Williams, Wayne Shorter and McCoy.

segments.title: Tony Williams's marijuana and Elvin's arrest
segments.summary: Elvin tells that Tony Williams gave the police his name and he was arrested in Hokkaido, and Keiko saw him handcuffed.

segments.title: Jail and trial in Japan, October 1966 to February 1967
segments.summary: Keiko and Elvin describe his detention, the trial, karate lessons from a guard and the deportation.

segments.title: Aftermath: returning to Japan and Kenny Clarke replacing him
segments.summary: The tour continued, Elvin lost drums, and Keiko took him back to Japan yearly to clear his name.

segments.title: Racism, Black GIs in Japan and his father's draft refusal
segments.summary: The talk moves to race, Black troops in Japan, and Elvin's father walking to Jackson to refuse the World War I draft.

segments.title: 'Putting It Together', his first Blue Note date as leader
segments.summary: Elvin calls this trio album a favorite, with Garrison's compositions, Farrell, and 'Keiko's Birthday March'.

segments.title: Touring and the Vanguard with the new trio
segments.summary: The album led to European tours and extended Village Vanguard engagements arranged with Max Gordon.

segments.title: Billy Taylor's liner notes and the Jazzmobile
segments.summary: Elvin praises Billy Taylor and describes concerts on the back of a truck in Harlem.

segments.title: 'Heavy Sounds', 'Dear John C.' and Charlie Mariano
segments.summary: Elvin sorts out these albums, saying 'Dear John C.' was more Charlie Mariano's date.

segments.title: Jimmy Garrison's troubles and leaving the trio
segments.summary: Garrison's trouble over his girlfriend and wife led to jail, and Elvin and Keiko helped him.

segments.title: 'Heavy Sounds' with Richard Davis and 'Summertime'
segments.summary: Larry Coryell did not show, so Richard Davis improvised 'Summertime' on bow and Bob Thiele recorded it.

segments.title: New lineups: Grossman, Liebman, Perla and 'Poly Curtains'
segments.summary: After Garrison left, he used Gene Clark, then Steve Grossman, Dave Liebman and Gene Perla, still without a pianist.

segments.title: Keiko's tune 'Shinjitsu', 'Mr. Jones' and their marriage
segments.summary: Keiko explains writing 'Shinjitsu', her culture shock, the 'Mr. Jones' album, and their February 16 anniversary.

segments.title: Acting in the film 'Zachariah'
segments.summary: Albert Goldman's article led to a Hollywood call; Elvin took horse-riding lessons and filmed in Mexico for three weeks.

segments.title: The drum battle with Ginger Baker at the Lyceum
segments.summary: A Melody Maker spat led to a London concert with Ginger Baker's Air Force, then a tour.

segments.title: Mitch Mitchell's visit with a carved name
segments.summary: Brown tells how Mitch Mitchell was inspired by Elvin; Mitchell visited in 1973 and left a carving.

segments.title: Elvin's influence on rock drummers
segments.summary: Brown argues Mitchell and Bonham carry Elvin's concept of time into rock; Elvin says no one had said this.

segments.title: First playing in London, at Ronnie Scott's
segments.summary: He recalls the all-night club and meeting Tubby Hayes and others, in 1968.

segments.title: Hearing of Coltrane's death and his offers of help
segments.summary: Bob Thiele called Elvin to say Trane had died, and Elvin recalls Trane's offers of money and the Chelsea Hotel years.

segments.title: Jimmy Garrison's last visit and the Vienna anthem
segments.summary: Elvin recalls Garrison's last request for money and his wife, and the Vienna request to play the national anthem.

segments.title: Miles asks what to pay David Liebman
segments.summary: On a break he tells how Miles asked what to pay Liebman, and they remain friends.

segments.title: What makes a recording session succeed
segments.summary: He says players must make a commitment, and a studio is more impersonal than a bandstand.

segments.title: What he looks for in musicians for his band
segments.summary: He wants maturity, command of the instrument, and sincerity, judging by hearing them play.

segments.title: Handling substitutes
segments.summary: He insists he must know who a sub is and will play without them rather than accept a stranger.

segments.title: Qualities of a bandleader
segments.summary: He says a leader needs understanding of people and should not ask what he cannot do himself.

segments.title: What the Army gave him: self-discipline
segments.summary: He says the Army gave him self-discipline.

segments.title: Musicians who come back to his band
segments.summary: Elvin says he trusts his players like Ellington did, letting them leave and return.

segments.title: Beginnings of the Elvin Jones Jazz Machine
segments.summary: He says the Jazz Machine began with Garrison and Farrell, with members changing over the years.

segments.title: 'Very Rare' and reissue practice
segments.summary: He objects to a reissue mixing tracks from different groups.

segments.title: Keiko's compositions and musical background
segments.summary: Keiko explains her tune 'Zangee', her violin and Japanese folk music, and writing from Elvin's drumming.

segments.title: Keiko as drum tech and tuner
segments.summary: Keiko tells how she learned to tune Elvin's drums, taking nine years to get a piano-like tone.

segments.title: Future plans and passing the music on
segments.summary: Elvin is content to keep playing, and Keiko discusses training young players.

segments.title: What music means to him; tape change
segments.summary: After a tape break Elvin says music means doing the work he was born to do.

segments.title: His leg bypass surgery
segments.summary: Elvin explains the arterial bypass for his circulation problems, done November 2001, and his recovery and diet.

segments.title: Closing thanks
segments.summary: Anthony Brown thanks Elvin and Keiko for the interview.

segments.title: September 11 from their apartment
segments.summary: Keiko and Elvin describe watching the second plane and trying to get home.

segments.title: Elvin's thoughts on terrorism and religion
segments.summary: He reflects on the attacks and religion; Keiko fears another.

segments.title: The master class at the Manhattan School of Music
segments.summary: He describes a lively jam with students.

segments.title: Teaching drum students
segments.summary: Elvin explains his view of the teacher's role, his students, and a short teaching stint around 1972.

segments.title: Upcoming Blue Note dates and goodbye
segments.summary: Brown asks about the Blue Note engagement with Cecil Taylor and the interview ends.
